question: Describe a time when you improved morale and productivity on your team. What were the underlying problems and their causes? How did you prevent them from negatively impacting the team in the future?

raiseTranscript.text: Our sprint had unclear ticket priorities and I kept getting pulled into last-minute asks. I raised it in standup, proposed a simple priority matrix, and after the manager approved I started using it on my own work and shared the template.
What was the root cause?
New PM was still ramping and didn't know our capacity. I asked for a 15-min sync each Monday to align.
Did it stick?
We did it for the next three sprints; morale on my tickets improved because I stopped context-switching.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe time you improved morale/productivity
Situation: unclear priorities from new PM, candidate's own tickets suffered
Action: built simple matrix, proposed weekly sync, applied to own work first
Outcome: three sprints of better focus; shared template
Quote: "I asked for a 15-min sync each Monday to align"
Follow-up: root cause was PM ramp; candidate owned the ask
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. The candidate owned a local process gap instead of waiting for direction and used a lightweight mechanism to protect their own output. They correctly identified the cause (new PM ramp) and created a repeatable sync rather than a one-off fix. The story stays within individual scope yet shows initiative to make the change durable. Biggest strength is the willingness to surface the issue directly and test a fix on their own work before broadcasting it.

lowerTranscript.text: The team was stressed because leadership kept changing priorities every week. I tried to keep my head down and just work faster.
What did you do to improve morale?
I complained in the retro that priorities were bad. Nothing really changed after that.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe time you improved morale/productivity
Situation: weekly priority changes
Action: worked harder, complained in retro
Outcome: no change mentioned
Quote: "I tried to keep my head down"
Follow-up: no root-cause analysis or personal ownership of a fix
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. The candidate attributed the problem entirely to leadership and took no concrete action beyond venting in a retro. There is no evidence of attempting to understand the cause or testing a local solution. The response shows passivity rather than ownership of their own productivity and morale.

raiseTranscript.text: Two teams were duplicating work on the same data pipeline because handoff meetings kept getting canceled. I scheduled a joint working session, mapped the overlap, and proposed a shared ownership model with a single on-call rotation.
How did you get buy-in?
I showed both teams the duplicated tickets and the velocity loss in the last quarter. One eng manager agreed to pilot the rotation for a month.
What prevented recurrence?
We added a recurring 30-min sync and a shared backlog tag so future work was visible before tickets were created.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe time you improved morale/productivity
Situation: duplicated pipeline work across two teams
Action: ran joint session, quantified overlap, proposed shared on-call
Outcome: one-month pilot, recurring sync added
Quote: "I showed both teams the duplicated tickets and the velocity loss"
Follow-up: used data to gain cross-team agreement
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. The candidate used concrete data to surface duplicated effort and drove a cross-team process change without formal authority. They addressed the root cause (missing visibility and handoff) by creating a lightweight recurring mechanism. The story demonstrates influence and a durable fix rather than a heroic one-time effort. Biggest strength is turning a morale-draining overlap into a shared ownership model.

lowerTranscript.text: Our team was burned out from too many projects. I told my manager we should drop some work but nothing happened.
Did you talk to the other teams?
I mentioned it once in a leadership meeting but didn't follow up.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe time you improved morale/productivity
Situation: team burnout from too many projects
Action: told manager, mentioned once in meeting
Outcome: no change
Quote: "I mentioned it once in a leadership meeting but didn't follow up"
Follow-up: no cross-team coordination or data-driven proposal
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for senior. The candidate identified a cross-team problem but limited action to a single mention without follow-through or data. No attempt to influence peers or create a shared solution. The response shows recognition without the ownership or persistence expected at this level.

raiseTranscript.text: After two high performers left, exit interviews showed lack of growth paths. I ran a skills-mapping exercise with the team, created two new project leads roles, and started monthly career conversations.
How did you handle underperformers during this?
One engineer was coasting; I gave clear expectations and a 30-day plan. They improved and later took one of the lead roles.
What made it stick?
I tied the new roles to promotion criteria and had the team vote on the first pilot project so ownership felt earned.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe time you improved morale/productivity
Situation: two high-performer exits due to unclear growth
Action: skills map, created lead roles, monthly 1:1s, handled one underperformer with plan
Outcome: improved retention, one underperformer promoted
Quote: "I tied the new roles to promotion criteria"
Follow-up: addressed underperformance directly while building growth paths
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. The candidate connected attrition to a structural gap, created roles with clear criteria, and handled underperformance with a documented plan rather than avoidance. They involved the team in shaping the solution, increasing buy-in. The story shows both people development and process leverage. Biggest strength is using exit data to drive role redesign while still managing performance issues transparently.

lowerTranscript.text: Team morale was low after a reorg. I sent an email saying I was there to support them and held an all-hands.
A couple people still left but the rest seemed okay after the meeting.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe time you improved morale/productivity
Situation: post-reorg morale drop
Action: sent email, held all-hands
Outcome: some attrition, rest "seemed okay"
Quote: "I sent an email saying I was there to support them"
Follow-up: no individual plans or structural changes
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for manager. The response relies on one-way communication and lacks evidence of diagnosing root causes or creating targeted development actions. Underperformance and growth concerns are not addressed. The candidate did not demonstrate the coaching or structural leverage expected of a people manager.

raiseTranscript.text: After acquiring a company, integration created two competing roadmaps and duplicated platforms. I formed a joint steering group, ran a six-week portfolio review, and consolidated to one platform with clear ownership.
How did you manage the politics?
I made the trade-off explicit: keep both and miss next-year revenue target, or consolidate and protect margins. Both original leads kept scope on the surviving platform.
Long-term prevention?
We added a quarterly portfolio health review with P&L owners and a rule that any new initiative above $2M must go through the same process.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe time you improved morale/productivity
Situation: post-acquisition roadmap conflict and duplication
Action: joint steering group, six-week review, consolidated platform, protected original leads' scope
Outcome: single platform, protected margins
Quote: "I made the trade-off explicit: keep both and miss next-year revenue target"
Follow-up: institutionalized quarterly review and threshold rule
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. The candidate framed a high-ambiguity integration problem around concrete business outcomes (revenue and margins) and created a durable governance mechanism rather than a one-time decision. They managed competing interests by making trade-offs transparent and preserving scope for key leaders. The story shows strategic judgment and org-level leverage. Biggest strength is turning a trust-eroding duplication into a repeatable portfolio process.

lowerTranscript.text: We had low morale after missing targets. I told the org we would focus on fewer priorities next quarter.
What structural change did you make?
I asked VPs to reduce their project lists. Some did, some didn't.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe time you improved morale/productivity
Situation: missed targets, low morale
Action: told org to focus, asked VPs to cut projects
Outcome: inconsistent follow-through
Quote: "I asked VPs to reduce their project lists. Some did, some didn't"
Follow-up: no governance or accountability mechanism created
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for exec. The candidate communicated intent but created no mechanism to enforce or sustain the change across the organization. Trade-offs were not made explicit and no durable process was installed. The response lacks the strategic leverage and long-term thinking required at this level.

diagnostic.manager: Links attrition to missing growth paths
